1.why: All six screens are static two-panel pages with no animations, moving images, or pop-ups.

2.why: Bold headings, coloured callout boxes, and solid blue buttons make key elements stand out, although the dark sidebar logs panel is visually as prominent as the main task card.

3.why: Each step places one labelled input and one primary button in the same spot and keeps the needed codes visible in the sidebar, so the user can locate what she needs quickly.

4.why: The numbered step indicator, on-screen password rules, and visible tokens mean the user mostly recognizes rather than recalls, though she must still remember her account contact and the new password unaided.

5.why: No password manager support, autofill hint, or remember-me option appears on any of the six screens.

6.why: The interface shows no saved or familiar items because the contact value is explicitly not displayed or retained, leaving only the newly generated log entries to recognize.

7.why: Sentences are short and legible, but technical terms such as recovery token and multi-factor authentication reduce clarity for a 67-year-old user.

8.why: No error message is visible in any screenshot, so there is no evidence that errors describe the problem and how to fix it; only proactive instructions are shown.

9.why: The contact and password fields give rules but no example input, while the sidebar logs effectively show the exact token and MFA code to type.

10.why: The flow mandates a single password-plus-token-plus-MFA path and never offers alternative choices such as password, code, or face login.

11.why: Every screen presents at most one input field and one primary button, so the user is never faced with too many choices at one time.

12.why: Outcomes are communicated through step transitions, the updated test logs, and explicit confirmations like Privacy statement accepted, although failure outcomes are never shown.

13.why: Each new step opens with a short explanatory tip box and a persistent anti-phishing reminder in the sidebar.

14.why: A Return to recovery request link lets the user retry the token step, but no visible error or retry feedback is shown for mistyped tokens, codes, or passwords.

15.why: All six screens reuse the same header, two-card layout, callout style, button styling, and sidebar, making the design highly consistent.
